sources.news_title: U.S. extends Ebola travel ban to green card holders | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
U.S. extends Ebola travel ban to green card holders
WASHINGTON >> The United States on Friday temporarily banned the entry of lawful permanent residents who have been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days, citing concerns over Ebola.
U.S. citizens, nationals and green card holders had been exempt from a 30-day Ebola ban, but the CDC said Friday that extending the ban to green card holders was necessary to stop the virus from entering the country.
“Applying this authority to lawful permanent residents for a limited period of time provides a balance between protecting public health and managing emergency response resources,” the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement.
The World Health Organization on Friday raised to “very high” the risk of the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola turning into a national outbreak in the DRC and has declared the outbreak there and in Uganda an emergency of international concern.
The CDC first issued the order on Monday under Title 42 of U.S. public health law, which allows federal health authorities to prohibit migrants from entering the country to prevent the spread of contagious diseases.
Green card holders have historically been shielded from U.S. entry restrictions. The CDC’s COVID-era Title 42 order did not apply to them, nor have President Donald Trump’s various travel bans.

sources.news_title: Trump administration expands Ebola travel restrictions to green card holders
U.S. expands Ebola-related entry restrictions to include green card holders
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES, May 23 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Friday that lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders, will now be subject to temporary entry restrictions related to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in East and Central Africa.
The expanded restrictions follow an interim final rule issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services that revises federal public health guidelines to prevent the introduction of dangerous communicable diseases into the United States.
Under the new rule, green card holders who have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan within the past 21 days will be temporarily barred from entering the United States, according to the CDC.
The agency said the measure expands the scope of Ebola-related entry restrictions announced earlier this week. On Monday, the CDC unveiled a 30-day package of enhanced public health measures, including strengthened traveler screening and monitoring, as well as entry restrictions on certain non-U.S. passport holders who had recently traveled to Ebola-affected areas.
The CDC stressed that the new rule does not permanently prohibit green card holders from returning to the United States. Rather, it grants the agency discretionary authority to temporarily restrict entry when necessary to protect public health and manage emergency response resources.
The CDC said no Ebola cases linked to the current outbreak have been reported in the United States, and the immediate risk to the general public remains low. ■

sources.news_title: Uganda confirms fresh Ebola cases as US extends Green Card travel restrictions
sources.text:
Uganda confirms fresh Ebola cases as US extends Green Card travel restrictions
What you need to know:
- Uganda races to contain Ebola as WHO sounds alarm over DR Congo outbreak.
Uganda’s Ministry of Health on Saturday confirmed three new Ebola infections, raising the country’s total number of confirmed cases to five, barely 24 hours after the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that the outbreak in neighbouring DR Congo (DRC) risked spiralling into a national epidemic.
In a press statement issued by the Director General Health Services, Prof Charles Olaro, the ministry on Saturday said the new infections involve a Ugandan driver who transported the country’s first confirmed Ebola patient, a Ugandan health worker who treated the initial case, and a Congolese woman who travelled into Uganda from the DR Congo.
The Congolese patient reportedly entered Uganda through Arua after falling ill in the DRC and later travelled to Kampala aboard a chartered flight, where she sought treatment at a private hospital on May 10.
Although she was discharged in stable condition and returned to the DRC on May 14, Ugandan authorities later traced and tested her after receiving a tip-off from the pilot who airlifted her. The sample later tested positive for Ebola.
Health officials said the two Ugandan patients had already been identified among known contacts and were under follow-up.
“All contacts linked to the confirmed cases have since been identified and are being closely monitored and followed up by response teams,” the ministry said, urging the public to remain calm but vigilant.
The latest developments come amid mounting international concern over the spread of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in eastern Congo.
This is a rare strain for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
The WHO last Sunday declared the outbreak an emergency of international concern, before escalating its risk assessment on Friday.
“We are now revising our risk assessment to very high at the national level, high at the regional level, and low at global level,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters.
According to WHO figures, Congo has so far recorded 82 confirmed Ebola cases, seven confirmed deaths, 177 suspected deaths and nearly 750 suspected infections.
“The potential of this virus spreading rapidly is high, very high, and that changed the whole dynamic,” said Abdirahman Mahamud.
Despite the growing regional alarm, WHO officials said Uganda’s aggressive response measures, including intense contact tracing, surveillance and the cancellation of mass gatherings like the annual June 3 Martyr’s Day, appear to have slowed local transmission.
Uganda’s Ministry of Health said surveillance, case management and public awareness campaigns had been intensified to contain the outbreak and protect the population.
US extends Ebola travel ban to Green Card holders
The United States on Friday temporarily extended its Ebola-related travel ban to include lawful permanent residents, commonly known as Green Card holders, who have recently travelled through DR Congo, Uganda or South Sudan.
Previously, U.S. citizens, nationals and permanent residents had been exempted from a 30-day Ebola restriction order.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the expansion was necessary to reduce the risk of the virus entering the country.
“Applying this authority to lawful permanent residents for a limited period of time provides a balance between protecting public health and managing emergency response resources,” the CDC said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Uganda’s Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health, Dr Diana Atwine, told envoys during a Friday meeting that the country urgently requires at least Shs90 billion to sustain Ebola containment operations over the next three months as the threat along the usually porous Uganda-DR Congo border intensifies.
“We want to continue empahsizieng that we’ve value for the resources provided. Uganda is open to supporting DR Congo,” she added.

sources.news_title: Green-card holders who travelled to Ebola-affected Congo, Uganda, South Sudan now can't reenter US: CDS
sources.text:
US health authorities said they plan to temporarily bar permanent residents of the country from reentering if they’ve traveled recently to Ebola-affected areas in a new rule published Friday.
The move escalates the Trump administration’s reliance on travel restrictions in response to the fast-spreading outbreak in central Africa linked to hundreds of cases and 177 suspected deaths.
The revision to quarantine rules lets the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention block lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green-card holders, from entering if they’ve traveled to countries where the virus is spreading.
That would intensify the restrictions announced earlier this week barring travel to the US for people who had been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the prior 21 days. That order didn’t apply to US citizens, nationals or lawful permanent residents.
The CDC said in a statement that the rule won’t permanently bar affected green-card holders but provides the agency the authority to restrict entry when necessary. The rule said the decision stems from resource constraints and the fact that green-card holders are more likely to have ties to people who live outside the US, making their inability to return to US soil less burdensome.
The Department of Human and Health Services and the CDC “have determined that the best balance between ensuring the Director of CDC has the ability to properly allocate resources and taking into account the interests of persons entering the United States is to draw the line at lawful permanent residents,” the rule said.
The interim final rule published late Friday is effective immediately and will remain in effect for six months or until Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. determines it is no longer needed.
Existing measures “have not completely stopped (and will not completely stop) global travelers, and other persons crossing from one country into another country, from spreading Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus across country boundaries,” the interim rule said. The broader authority “is therefore critical to slowing the introduction of Ebola disease into the United States.”
The Trump administration has emphasized travel restrictions and enhanced screening in its response to the Ebola outbreak. Those measures have drawn some criticism from health authorities in the region who have urged the international community to boost efforts to contain the outbreak. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention decried the travel restrictions, saying they’re often unnecessary and ineffective.
The order also followed a Trump administration rule change requiring that permanent residents in the US will now have to leave the country to apply for green cards.

sources.news_title: Federal rule expands ability to limit entry during dangerous disease outbreaks, CDC says
sources.text:
Federal rule expands ability to limit entry during dangerous disease outbreaks, CDC says
RAPID CITY, S.D. (KOTA) - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Friday that a new federal public health rule will allow temporary limits on entry into the United States for some lawful permanent residents during certain disease outbreaks.
The rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services under Title 42 authority, expands the government’s ability to temporarily restrict entry during public health emergencies involving dangerous communicable diseases.
Under the updated policy, lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders, may face temporary entry restrictions under limited circumstances tied to specific disease outbreaks.
Federal officials said the current action is connected to the ongoing Ebola outbreak response. Lawful permanent residents who have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan within the previous 21 days could be subject to temporary restrictions under the order.
Health officials emphasized the measure is not a permanent prohibition on returning to the United States. Instead, the revised authority gives the CDC flexibility to temporarily limit entry when necessary and legally permitted to protect public health.
The agency said the limited use of the authority is intended to balance disease prevention efforts with managing emergency response resources during rapidly evolving outbreaks.

sources.news_title: HHS rule bars green card holders who visited Ebola zones from entering US
sources.text:
WASHINGTON— A new federal rule from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) now temporarily restricts lawful permanent residents who have recently been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan from entering the United States, due to the current Ebola outbreak.
Under the revised rule, green card holders who had been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan within the previous 21 days are blocked from entering the United States, according to an announcement by HHS and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The agencies explained the rule does not permanently stop lawful permanent residents from returning to the country. Instead, it gives the CDC discretion to restrict entry for a limited time when the law allows it and when officials say public health conditions require it.
Federal health officials said the change is meant to balance disease control with emergency response demands.
They also said fast-moving outbreaks involving highly dangerous diseases require that option. Officials explained some lawful permanent residents may travel more often to affected areas because of close family or community connections abroad, which could raise the risk of exposure.

HHS expands CDC power to temporarily block some travelers amid Ebola outbreak
FRESNO, Calif. (FOX26) — Federal health officials have expanded the government’s authority to temporarily block certain travelers from entering the United States amid the current Ebola outbreak, including some lawful permanent residents.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services issued an interim final which temporarily limits the entry of specific people into the United States to help stop the spread of dangerous diseases.
Under the revised rule, the ability to suspend introduction into the United States now applies to U.S. lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.
Given the current Ebola outbreak, lawful permanent residents who have been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan within the last 21 days are prevented from entering the United States.
The rule does not permanently bar lawful permanent residents from returning to the United States.
Instead, it gives the CDC discretionary authority to restrict entry when needed and allowed by law.
Officials said applying this authority to lawful permanent residents for a limited period of time is intended to balance protecting public health with managing emergency response resources.
During rapidly evolving outbreaks of highly dangerous diseases, officials said the option is required to protect public health.
The rule also notes that some lawful permanent residents may have close family or community ties abroad and may travel more frequently to affected regions, which can increase the chance of exposure to disease.

sources.news_title: Trump admin pauses even more US visas due to Ebola outbreak
sources.text:
The U.S. State Department confirmed Friday that it was expanding its Ebola-related visa pause, as health officials continue to struggle to bring the outbreak in parts of Africa under control.
In an update shared with Newsweek, first seen by The Wall Street Journal, the Trump administration said it was planning to pause issuing visas to anyone who had been to an affected country within three weeks, after already suspending visa issuances at the respective embassies.
The U.S. was forced to make similar changes during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, amid efforts to stop the spread of the virus, for which there was no vaccine yet.
A State Department official told Newsweek that the Trump Administration was protecting the country and Americans, by upholding public health standards through the visa process.
Which Countries Are Impacted By the Expanded Pause?
Potential immigrants or visitors to the U.S. who have been to South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, or Uganda within the past 21 days will not be eligible for a visa while the pause is in place. That would expand the pause already imposed on visa issuance from the embassies in Juba, Kinshasa, and Kampala earlier this week.
The State Department said May 18 that the pause applies to those seeking immigrant and nonimmigrant visas, including those traveling for tourism, business, and study.
Why Are Appointments Being Canceled?
"The Department of State is committed to ensuring that its visa process upholds the highest standards for U.S. public health and safety," a press release from the State Department read on May 18.
A similar reason was given for the planned expansion of the restrictions: to stop the spread of the disease.
The move echoes efforts in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the U.S. sought to restrict visa approvals for those from affected countries, to try to slow the spread.
When Will the Pause Be Lifted?
As of Friday afternoon, this was unclear, as concerns about the virus seemed to be increasing. The State Department had said Monday that it would reach out to applicants with any updates.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said Friday that the outbreak was posing a “very high" risk for Congo, although the risk of the disease spreading globally remained low.
Eighty-two cases and seven deaths have been confirmed in Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, but the outbreak was believed to be “much larger."
With no vaccine available yet for the Bundibugyo virus, which spread undetected for weeks in Congo's Ituri Province, there are now 750 suspected cases and 177 suspected deaths across the region.
How Contagious Is Ebola?
Ebola can infect humans when they have been in close contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected animals—usually fruit bats, chimpanzees, gorillas, monkeys, forest antelope, or porcupines found ill or dead or in the rainforest.
Dr. Paul Spiegel, director of the Center for Humanitarian Health at Johns Hopkins University, previously told Newsweek that direct risk to Americans right now is "low," as Ebola is not airborne, and the Bundibugyo strain driving this outbreak spreads only through contact with the bodily fluids of someone who already has symptoms.
Current CDC Guidelines on Travel
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Thursday that it was imposing new health restrictions on those who had recently been to the three affected countries, requiring them to arrive exclusively through Washington Dulles International Airport for screening.
Officials warned passengers of possible flight changes or cancellations as airlines adjust to the measures.
The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority previously told Newsweek it was coordinating with federal agencies to support the expanded health measures.
“The Airports Authority is working with federal partners to support efforts led by the Centers for Disease Control affecting various international flights arriving at Dulles Airport. This includes providing staff and public safety resources as needed. We are not expecting any significant impacts on airport customers,” the authority said.

US to Keep Out Green-Card Holders With Ebola-Area Travel
CDC says green card holders who were recently in countries where Ebola is spreading can’t reenter US
How did U.S. restrict Ebola travelers?
sources.text:
How did U.S. restrict Ebola travelers?
Travel limits and screening steps
The U.S. response to the Ebola outbreak described in these stories includes multiple layers of restrictions for people returning from Ebola-affected countries. Measures reported include rerouting flights, requiring arrivals at a specific airport for U.S.-bound passengers, and restricting entry for certain noncitizens who may have been exposed.
Several related updates show the approach evolving as officials tried to prevent the virus from entering the country and to standardize medical monitoring:
- Rerouting of U.S. passengers: American travelers returning from Ebola-affected countries were directed to specific routing rather than arriving at multiple destinations.
- Single-airport requirement: A Department of Homeland Security requirement directed returning passengers to arrive at Washington-Dulles International Airport for screening/testing.
- Entry restrictions expanded: The administration planned to block entry for more noncitizens who may have been exposed after they had been in countries affected by Ebola.
Why those steps matter
The intent of these rules is to increase the likelihood that potentially exposed people are identified quickly and monitored in a controlled setting. That can reduce the chance that an outbreak grows undetected after arrival.
At the same time, coverage in the story set includes criticism and rights concerns from Congo health officials and also mentions scrutiny about how restrictions affect volunteers and affected travelers. Those reactions highlight that public health measures often trigger political and ethical debates—especially when rules are broad or disruptive.
What’s the practical impact?
For passengers, the changes mean more time for screening, potential quarantine or monitoring, and less flexibility in travel plans. For health systems, concentrating arrivals at one airport can streamline testing capacity and contact follow-up.
Overall, these stories depict a strategy focused on preventing importation through destination control and targeted monitoring rather than relying solely on case-by-case decisions after arrival.

sources.text:
Published 05/21/26 at 9:45 a.m.
By Oregon Coast Beach Connection Staff
(Portland, Oregon) – The recent outbreak of a new strain of Ebola has the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring a “a public health emergency of international concern,“ as the U.S. monitors a handful of citizens there who were exposed. (Above: Portland International Airport / Oregon Coast Beach Connection)
What it means to most countries around the world is some travel limitations, at least for now. At home, in Oregon and Washington, neither of the health departments in the Pacific Northwest have issued any statements.
However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said they are implementing new health measures to prevent the introduction of Ebola Virus Disease linked to the Bundibugyo strain, due to the ongoing outbreaks in East Africa. The agency issued the 30-day order on May 18. See CDC and DHS latest on Ebola
According to the CDC, federal agencies including the DHS will expand health screening and traveler monitoring for people arriving from affected regions. Travel and entry restrictions will apply to non-U.S. citizens who have been in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, or South Sudan within the past 21 days.
“At this time, CDC assesses the immediate risk to the general U.S. public as low, but we will continue to evaluate the evolving situation and may adjust public health measures as additional information becomes available,” CDC said.
The agency is also coordinating with airlines and port-of-entry officials to identify travelers who may have been exposed, while increasing contact tracing, laboratory capacity, and hospital readiness across the country. CDC personnel will continue supporting outbreak response efforts overseas.
